deep.reconstruction:
The page is printed text from Christian Leiste's arithmetic textbook (Wolfenbüttel, about 1790), in the chapter on compound proportion (§§138–142). Its only manuscript content is Gauss's left-margin numerals, which carry over from his lemniscatic computation on the previous page.

(0) End of a mechanics remark. A man moves a load some number of feet and a horse twice as far. For the most advantageous use of force one should take only 4/9 'der Geschwindigkeit'. This presumably comes from the Euler/D. Bernoulli law F(v) = K(1 - v/c)^2. The power P(v) = K v (1 - v/c)^2 has dP/dv = K(1 - v/c)(1 - 3v/c) = 0, giving v = c/3. At that speed the force is F = (4/9)K. So the textbook's 4/9 is properly a fraction of the maximal force, not of the speed (my interpretation; see errors).

(1) The text notes that the formulas of §138 and §141 also serve for setting up a problem by Rees's rule (the 'Reesische Regel', i.e. the chain rule or Kettensatz). For the preceding example, q = l s w and L S W = P give q = l s w P/(L S W). Numerically q = 16·15·4·6/(9·20·3) = 5760/540 = 32/3 (the evaluation is mine; the book gives only the quotient).

(2) Example 4, carrier's wage. A carrier is to haul 36 hundredweight (Ctn.) for 30 Meilen at 7½ Rthlr per 3 Ctn. The wage is assumed proportional to weight × distance, so the full job pays 36·7.5/3 = 90 Rthlr.
- Leg 1: 36 Ctn for 8 Meilen pays 90·8/30 = 24.
- Leg 2: after unloading 12 Ctn, 24 Ctn go 9 Meilen. Using LS : ls = P : p, 36·30 : 24·9 = 90 : p, so p = 90·216/1080 = 18.
- Leg 3: he reloads 8 Ctn, so 32 Ctn go the remaining 30 - 8 - 9 = 13 Meilen. Then p = 90·32·13/1080 = 104/3 = 34⅔ Rthlr = 34 Rthlr 16 gGr (24 gGr = 1 Rthlr).
- Total: 24 + 18 + 34⅔ = 76⅔ Rthlr, on the assumption that the cost of unloading falls on him alone.

(3) Example 5, inverse compound proportion. Effort is constant (E = e), so C·T = c·t. Here C = 20 workers, T = 15 weeks · 6 days · 6 hours, c = 36, t = x · 6 · 8. Then 20·15·6·6 = 36·x·6·8, so x = 10800/1728 = 25/4 = 6¼ weeks.

(4) Example 6, interest-free reciprocal loan. B lends 1000 Rthlr for 7½ months. In return A must lend 1500 Rthlr for t months with C·T = c·t, giving t = 5 months. The problem continues on the next page.

(5) Gauss's margin. The numerals continue his work on the previous page, where he sought a rational (Padé-type) approximant to the lemniscatic sine:
sl x ≈ x(1 - x^4/60 + …)/(1 + x^4/12 + …), with sl x = x - x^5/10 + x^9/120 - 11x^13/15600 + …
The margin entries correspond to the previous page's '14.13.12.600' (= 1310400) and '23814000 / 229', and to its column of seven- and eight-digit numbers (3768323, 3598355, 50169968, 4180830, 3904092, 50305697, 4192141, …). These are evidently trial or verification products or quotients in that coefficient determination. Their exact role cannot be reconstructed from this page alone.
errors: Printed text: '4/9 der Geschwindigkeit' sits oddly with the standard Euler/Bernoulli result. Under F = K(1 - v/c)^2 the optimum is v = c/3, and it is the force that is 4/9 of maximum. This is possibly a textbook slip, or the preceding page frames it differently (not visible here).
All the arithmetic on the page (examples 4, 5, 6 and the chain-rule quotient) checks correctly.
The previous-page transcription has p = 2/3 against a printed or margin 'q'. That is outside this page; Gauss's margin numbers here give no independent check.

results.what: Optimal working speed or load for a man or horse: maximum power at v = c/3, force 4/9 of maximum
results.modern_name: Maximization of power for the force law F = K(1 - v/c)^2

results.what: Compound proportion (CT = ct, LS : ls = P : p) and Rees's chain rule
results.modern_name: Compound rule of three / chain rule (Kettensatz)
results.usually_credited_to: Traditional; Kettensatz attributed to C. F. von Rees (1739)

results.what: Gauss margin: continuation of the numerical work on a rational approximation of the lemniscatic sine
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss's lemniscate studies (1797ff.) are well known; Padé approximants are formalized by Padé (1892)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is printed textbook arithmetic. Gauss's only contribution is spill-over numerals from his known lemniscatic-function computations, with no new derivation legible here.

checkable.asserts: The chain-rule example evaluates to q = 32/3
Third leg pays 34 2/3 Rthlr = 34 Rthlr 16 gGr
Critical points of the power are v = c/3 (maximum) and v = c; at v = c/3, (1 - v/c)^2 = 4/9
Gives x - x^5/10 + x^9/120 + O(x^10), matching sl x = x - x^5/10 + x^9/120 (the context of Gauss's margin numbers)
Value of the margin product 14·13·12·600 from the lemniscate coefficient work
